content: Nine studies, involving a total of 3,881 participants, evaluated both Xpert Ultra and Xpert MTB/RIF for the detection of pulmonary tuberculosis (TB). For Xpert Ultra, a composite reference standard was used, which included clinical components as defined by the primary study authors. Eight studies, with 1,039 participants, assessed Xpert Ultra for the detection of rifampicin resistance. One study provided data for two cohorts, which were classified as separate studies (Mishra 2019a and Mishra 2019b). Most studies were judged to have high certainty of evidence. For the detection of active pulmonary TB in adults with signs and symptoms of the disease, an updated systematic review was conducted. Among children with signs and symptoms of pulmonary TB seeking care at healthcare facilities, the use of Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra as an initial diagnostic test for pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance was evaluated. The diagnostic accuracy of Xpert MTB/RIF for pulmonary TB and rifampicin resistance in children was compared with microbiological reference standards (MRS) and composite reference standards (CRS). The initial search identified 836 records, of which 707 were excluded. After full-text review, 50 studies were included in the quantitative meta-analysis. Of these, 40 studies (80%) were conducted in high TB burden countries, and 10 in high TB/HIV burden countries. For pulmonary TB detection, 43 studies evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of Xpert MTB/RIF in children, and three studies evaluated both Xpert Ultra and Xpert MTB/RIF. Forty-two studies used a culture-based reference standard, while one study used smear microscopy alone. Methodologically, most studies (83%) evaluating pulmonary TB had a low risk of bias in the patient selection domain. All studies had a low risk of bias in the index test domain, and 88% had a low risk of bias in the flow and timing domain. However, 47% of studies had an unclear risk of bias in the reference standard domain when using MRS, as only one culture was used to exclude TB. All studies using CRS had an unclear risk of bias due to the imperfect accuracy of the composite reference standard and varying definitions used by primary study authors. Regarding applicability, 50% of studies had high or unclear risk of bias in the patient selection domain because participants were evaluated exclusively as inpatients at tertiary care centers, or the clinical setting was unclear. Most studies (72%) had low concern for applicability in the index test domain due to standardized application of the index tests. Eleven studies evaluating stool as a specimen for Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra had an unclear risk of bias due to the absence of a standardized protocol for stool preparation. Applicability of the reference standard was considered a low concern for most studies (93%). For rifampicin resistance detection, six studies (223 participants) evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF, all conducted in high TB and multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) burden countries. Half of these studies had a low risk of bias in patient selection, and all had a low risk of bias in the reference standard domain. The reference standard was considered low risk if an automated process was used or if the results were interpreted without knowledge of the index tests. However, all six studies had applicability concerns regarding patient selection due to exclusive enrollment from inpatient or tertiary care centers. For the meta-analysis, 23 studies (6,612 participants) evaluated sputum specimens, 14 studies (3,468 participants) evaluated gastric specimens, four studies (1,125 participants) evaluated nasopharyngeal specimens, and 11 studies (1,592 participants) evaluated stool specimens. All these studies assessed Xpert MTB/RIF alone. Three studies (753 participants) evaluated both Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra on frozen sputum specimens, and one study (195 participants) evaluated both tests on nasopharyngeal specimens. No studies evaluated Xpert Ultra alone. The certainty of evidence for sensitivity and specificity was judged to be very low due to serious concerns about indirectness and imprecision. For extrapulmonary TB detection, 65 studies were included. A total of 63 studies (13,144 participants) evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF, including five that evaluated both Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert Ultra. These studies assessed Xpert MTB/RIF in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), lymph node aspirates, lymph node biopsies, pleural fluid, urine, synovial fluid, peritoneal fluid, pericardial fluid, and blood. Of the 65 studies, 39 (60%) were conducted in high TB burden countries, and 41 (63%) in high TB/HIV burden countries. Risk of bias was low in the domains of patient selection, index test, and flow and timing, but high or unclear in the reference standard domain due to decontamination of sterile specimens before culture inoculation. Applicability concerns were high or unclear in the patient selection domain for most studies due to exclusive evaluation of inpatients at tertiary care centers or unclear clinical settings. Six studies (507 participants) evaluated Xpert Ultra for extrapulmonary TB detection, using CSF, lymph node biopsy, pleural fluid, urine, and synovial fluid specimens. Evidence was generated in tertiary referral medical centers, and the certainty of evidence was judged to be low to very low due to imprecision and the small number of participants included in studies. For pulmonary TB diagnosis in adults in the general population, six surveys were identified, including data from four nationally representative and two subnational prevalence surveys. These surveys evaluated Xpert MTB/RIF or Xpert Ultra against a culture-based reference standard. The certainty of evidence was judged to be low for sensitivity and moderate for specificity due to concerns about indirectness and inconsistency.
